title: U.S. Employer Health Costs Set to Breach $19,000 Per Worker as Fourth Year of Near-Double-Digit Increases Looms
excerpt: Aon projects a 9.5% rise in 2027 healthcare spending, driven by GLP-1 drugs, chronic conditions, and AI-powered billing that inflates charges.
body:
• U.S. employer healthcare costs are projected to rise 9.5% in 2027, pushing average spending above $19,000 per employee, according to insurance broker Aon.
  • This marks the fourth consecutive year of near-double-digit increases, far outpacing inflation and wage growth.
  • GLP-1 drugs, rising chronic disease prevalence, and AI-driven clinical coding that inflates billed charges are key cost drivers.
  • Two-thirds of large employers plan to raise employee premium contributions in 2027, and nearly half will increase deductibles and copays.

American workers are about to feel another squeeze on their paychecks. Employer healthcare costs are projected to rise 9.5% in 2027, pushing the average cost above $19,000 per employee, insurance broker Aon reported on August 20.

It will be the fourth straight year of near-double-digit increases — a streak that has erased a decade of relatively moderate annual growth that averaged around 3%.

What Is Driving the Surge

Aon attributes the acceleration to several converging factors. Medical spending has climbed as patients use more healthcare services, chronic conditions become more prevalent, and the number of high-cost claims continues to increase. Greater use of specialty medicines and GLP-1 treatments for diabetes, obesity, and other conditions is adding significantly to prescription drug costs.

A newer and less expected driver has emerged: healthcare providers adopting artificial intelligence tools for clinical documentation and coding. According to Aon, more detailed AI-assisted coding is contributing to higher billed charges in some instances — effectively translating the same care into bigger invoices.

"Additional cost pressure is emerging as providers adopt technologies, including AI, that support more detailed clinical documentation and coding, contributing to higher billed charges in some instances."

— Aon report on 2027 employer healthcare projections

The Numbers

For 2026, employers are expected to cover about 82% of health-plan costs, with their share rising 8.8% to $14,432 per employee. Total plan costs — including the employee share — are projected to increase 8.3% to $17,562 this year.

Employees will spend an average of $5,297 in 2026, comprising $3,130 in payroll contributions and $2,167 in out-of-pocket expenses, a combined increase of 7.9% from the prior year.

Aon based its estimates on data from more than 1,100 U.S. employers covering 7.9 million employees and $135 billion in 2026 healthcare spending. The 9.5% projection for 2027 assumes employers do not make benefit changes or introduce care-management programs to curb expenses.

Employers Are Pushing Costs to Workers

Many will not sit still. A Mercer survey released earlier this summer found that two-thirds of large U.S. businesses plan to raise monthly premiums for employee health coverage through paycheck deductions in 2027. Nearly half — 48% of companies with 500 or more employees — said they will also increase deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums.

Some employers are dropping GLP-1 weight loss coverage altogether. While 49% of large employers covered these drugs in 2025, 6% dropped coverage in 2026 and another 5% are considering it for 2027, according to Mercer. Of those maintaining coverage, 27% said they have tightened or plan to tighten utilization controls.

The Wage Growth Drag

Rising health insurance costs are not just a benefits problem — they are dragging down wage growth. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that firms reported an average health cost increase of more than 13% in 2026. Absent those increases, businesses said they would have raised wages by roughly an additional percentage point on average.

The average wage increase for surveyed firms was 3.8%; without health cost pressure, it would have been 4.7%. That amounts to a 20% drag on wage growth, according to the Fed economists.

"Employers want to minimize increases in paycheck deductions while ensuring employees across all pay levels can afford the care they need, when they need it."

— Simon Camaj, Mercer's U.S. Health Leader

What It Means for Indian-American Workers

For Indian Americans working in the technology, healthcare, and financial services sectors — industries with traditionally generous benefits packages — the trend raises a practical question: how much of next year's raise will be eaten by insurance premiums? With family coverage premiums already approaching $27,000 annually, the gap between nominal pay increases and real take-home improvement continues to narrow.

Health policy researchers at KFF have found that two-thirds of the public now cite healthcare costs as their top financial worry, ranking it above utilities, food, rent, and mortgage payments.
nri_angle: Indian Americans in tech, healthcare, and finance sectors face rising premiums eating into pay raises as employer health costs hit near-double-digit annual growth.
